text:
Revealed: Full detail of Man City’s ‘irrefutable evidence’ as they look to overturn verdict
“Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.
 A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.
 City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:
 - Contemporaneous bank statements, government records and receipts they believe confirm the Abu Dhabi government as the source of funds for financing of deals
 - More recent evidence from the Abu Dhabi government reaffirming** **the accuracy of the original records
 - What they view as fundamental inconsistencies in the findings.
 Such a position could effectively be a high-stakes challenge to any appeal panel to question the legitimacy of official Abu Dhabi government documents.
 City lodged an appeal two weeks ago after the independent commission panel, which has never been individually identified, found the club guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules stretching back more than a decade.
 Sources with understanding of the Premier League’s case, however, express ongoing confidence in the verdict. In a league statement on September 29, it said “the commission has ruled (and an appeal board has confirmed) that the commission’s decision is a ‘final award’”.
 But in a short statement, the club said the commission’s ruling contained “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe”. The club added they had filed “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions”.
 The club are also understood to claim that the Premier League has no “smoking gun” or witnesses to the alleged wrongdoing, and is relying almost entirely on leaked emails.
 Crux of the matter
 Central to City’s appeal argument is that the panel overlooked almost all of their evidence that sponsorship payments came from the Abu Dhabi government, the shareholder of the sponsors.
 An appeal hearing date has yet to be set while a panel is appointed to scrutinise the evidence. In normal circumstances, the appeal commission has to return a decision, under Premier League rules, within 12 weeks. This gives a deadline of January 21.
 A possibility is that the appeal panel could refer the matter back to a new commission for a retrial.
 The independent commission ruled that City inflated commercial revenues and reduced costs by £920m, largely thanks to its ownership topping up “sham” sponsorship deals by more than £830m as part of a “disguised funding scheme”. The commission also found that the scheme was conducted without Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan being aware.
 The verdict sent shock waves through English football, led to calls for a criminal investigation and has prompted protests from rival fans at City’s Premier League matches.
 City’s case is that the money came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owner, and should therefore be treated as legitimate sponsorship revenue.
 Telegraph Sport detailed earlier this month how, during a US investigation into state-owned airlines, Etihad Airways stated: “The assertion that the Abu Dhabi government paid for Etihad’s sponsorship of English Premier League football club Manchester City is false.”
 City have pointed to the remarks being taken out of context and that the airline at the time went on to say that Etihad funded the sponsorship “from its own liquidity”, which is consistent with their position.
 Case for the defence
 The club presented three pillars of evidence around state funding at the hearing, which their lawyers claim were not given sufficient weight in terms of government funding involving sponsorship deals.
 Those pillars included contemporaneous documentation and bank statements from the Abu Dhabi government; letters from the government to the hearing confirming the accuracy of the original records; and witness evidence from club officials, senior figures at sponsors and government officials.
 City are expected to argue that the Premier League relied almost entirely on leaked emails and produced no direct witness. City have publicly stated that the panel’s approach contains “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact”, making the resulting findings “unsafe”.
 The commission previously “rejected that explanation” around government funding “as untrue”. “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the Club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme,” the panel said. City strongly dispute such a claim, believing proper tests were not applied.
 What could happen next
 Overturning the source-of-funds findings could have consequences for a substantial part of the case, as the accuracy of the club’s accounts directly affects the club’s compliance with the Premier League’s financial regulations. The extent of any impact would depend on which findings the appeal panel overturned and how the remaining charges were affected.
 The appeal panel can examine the commission’s decision, the documents submitted and transcripts of witness evidence. Witnesses are not generally re-examined, making the process different from a full rehearing. Possible outcomes include upholding the findings, overturning some or all of them, or referring matters back for further consideration.
 City also argue that the earlier Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling in 2020 supports their position, rejecting the suggestion that they escaped the Uefa case solely on a technicality that the case was time-barred and that specific findings were made by Cas that Etihad did not receive funds from Sheikh Mansour.
 There is unhappiness behind the scenes with the timing and presentation of the Premier League verdict, according to people familiar with the club’s position.

Official Guidelines for Conducting Yourself as a Manchester City Supporter
Following recent concerns from Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United supporters, it has become clear that Manchester City fans require additional guidance on how to behave appropriately.
 Fortunately, supporters of these three clubs have generously appointed themselves the moral guardians of English football, and it would be disrespectful not to acknowledge their authority.
 1. Celebrating goals
 Manchester City supporters must refrain from celebrating goals until permission has been granted by fans of Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United.
 A polite round of applause may be considered, but only once the goal has been independently assessed for financial irregularities.
 2. Celebrating victories
 Winning football matches is not, in itself, sufficient grounds for happiness.
 City supporters must first consider whether the result has caused emotional distress to supporters of historically significant football clubs.
 If so, celebrations should be postponed indefinitely.
 3. Discussing trophies
 City supporters are reminded that trophies won by Manchester City do not count and must not be brought up in football discussions.
 The legitimacy of any trophy is determined exclusively by whichever Liverpool or United supporter you happen to be arguing with.
 Arsenal supporters may also participate, provided the conversation does not involve European Cups.
 4. Expressing opinions
 City fans are permitted to have opinions about football, provided those opinions have been checked and approved by supporters of clubs with a greater number of Twitter followers.
 Disagreement with a Liverpool, Arsenal or United supporter is considered evidence of sportswashing.
 5. Attending matches
 City supporters must provide photographic evidence of their attendance, including a timestamp, GPS coordinates and a photograph of themselves holding that day's newspaper.
 Failure to do so will result in immediate classification as a plastic fan.
 Those who do attend must maintain a wholly solemn demeanour throughout. Smiling, cheering or displaying any outward signs of enjoyment may be interpreted as an attempt to legitimise financial misconduct.
 6. Showing respect for football's traditions
 City fans must respect the traditions established by English football's most prestigious institutions.
 These include breaking transfer records, spending hundreds of millions on players and expanding commercial revenues.
 However, City supporters must understand that these activities are only acceptable when undertaken by clubs who were already wealthy.
 7. Responding to rival supporters
 When told that City's achievements mean nothing, City supporters should simply thank the individual for taking time out of their day to explain this for the 4,000th time.
 Under no circumstances should City supporters point out that people who genuinely believe something is meaningless rarely spend eight hours a day talking about it.
 8. Understanding the independent moral hierarchy
 Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal supporters are to be treated as independent, impartial authorities on all matters involving Manchester City.
 Their decades of rivalry with City, personal dislike of the club and direct competitive interests do not constitute a conflict of interest.
 Suggesting otherwise is deeply disrespectful.
 9. Liverpool
 10. Accepting the correct level of punishment
 City supporters must accept that any punishment proposed by a rival supporter is both proportionate and legally sound.
 Points deductions, relegation, expulsion and the retrospective removal of trophies are all considered reasonable starting positions.
 The precise punishment will be determined by the number of angry replies beneath the latest unhinged journalist's tweet, which shall be treated as an authoritative interpretation of Premier League regulations.
 Questioning whether any of these punishments are actually available under the relevant regulations is considered further evidence of guilt.
 11. Accepting collective responsibility
 Manchester City supporters are reminded that they are personally responsible for all decisions made by the club's ownership, executives and legal representatives.
 Not knowing the details of a financial transaction undertaken in 2011 is no defence.
 Supporters are expected to have maintained comprehensive records of all sponsorship agreements, commercial arrangements and accounting practices throughout this period.
 Failure to produce these documents upon request from an Arsenal fan on Reddit will be interpreted as an admission of guilt.
 12. Respecting the appeals process
 City supporters must understand that whilst the right to appeal is a fundamental principle of justice, exercising that right is considered deeply inappropriate when Manchester City are involved.
 Any attempt to challenge a decision must be regarded as further evidence of wrongdoing, irrespective of the legal arguments presented.
 Supporters are reminded that the correct outcome of an appeal has already been determined by Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United fans, rendering the involvement of qualified legal professionals both entirely unnecessary and a flagrant waste of Premier League resources.
 13. Manchester United
 14. Demonstrating appropriate remorse
 Following any Manchester City victory, supporters must demonstrate a suitable degree of remorse.
 Acceptable responses include apologising to the opposition, acknowledging that the result is morally questionable and promising not to enjoy the next match.
 Supporters must not attempt to justify their happiness by referring to events that actually took place on the football pitch.
 15. Knowing when to remain silent
 City supporters must understand that silence is not an acceptable response to allegations, as it demonstrates complicity.
 Equally, responding to allegations is not acceptable, as it demonstrates a desperate attempt to defend the indefensible.
 Supporters are therefore advised to remain silent while simultaneously issuing a full and unconditional apology.
 Failure to comply will be taken as further evidence of guilt.
 16. Enjoying football
 Ultimately, Manchester City supporters are reminded that football is supposed to be enjoyed.
 Just not by you.
 Your role is to buy tickets, preferably not attend matches, support your team quietly and apologise whenever they win.
 Should you accidentally experience happiness, please report yourself to the nearest Liverpool, Arsenal or Manchester United supporter for immediate correction.
 17. Discussing football matches
 City supporters must understand that the events taking place during a football match are largely irrelevant to any subsequent discussion.
 Attempts to discuss tactics, individual performances or particularly well-worked goals should be discouraged.
 Supporters are reminded that the appropriate response to any Manchester City highlight is to mention the charges, regardless of whether they have any relevance to the footage.
 18. Recognising the importance of context
 City supporters must recognise that all achievements, performances and results must be viewed in their proper context.
 In practice, this means that positive developments involving Manchester City should be immediately qualified, dismissed or attributed to financial expenditure.
 Negative developments, however, may be discussed entirely on their own merits.
 19. Tottenham Hotspur
 City supporters must recognise Tottenham Hotspur as another vital guardian of English football's sporting integrity.
 While Tottenham supporters may not always participate in discussions concerning winning trophies, they remain exceptionally well qualified to advise others on how those trophies should be won.
 Their current league position must not be interpreted as a reflection of their expertise.
 Indeed, their willingness to prioritise the moral integrity of the competition over their own participation in it is to be commended.
 20. Manchester City
 City supporters must acknowledge that 20th place is the club's rightful position in the Premier League table.
 Supporters should understand that finishing bottom of the league with a mere minus 300 points would still represent an unacceptable degree of leniency. As a result all future matches involving the club are meaningless.
 Thank you for your cooperation.
 These guidelines are subject to change without notice, depending on Manchester City's latest result and the emotional wellbeing of rival supporters.

text:
Sponsorship Saga: The WHY?
The biggest question for me in the City scandal is still WHY?
 From what we know, between 2010/11 and 2017/18, City recorded around £950m in sponsorship from Abu Dhabi-linked companies, including Etihad. Of that, approximately £120m was actually paid by the sponsors themselves, with the remainder funded by ADUG through those sponsors.
 That means the sponsors directly contributed roughly 12.5% of the total.
 Let’s take the biggest example: Etihad’s shirt sponsorship, stadium naming rights and training campus naming rights, reportedly valued at £80m a year (in 2024).
 The reports don’t provide an exact breakdown of the funding for each deal. But, purely for the sake of argument, if we apply that 12.5% figure to the £80m valuation, we get just £10m a year in direct sponsor funding.
 Bear in mind that the £80m figure is already considered fair market value under the relevant FMV assessment parameters, on the assumption that the sponsorship was not owner-linked.
 So here’s the question: why structure, or continue to structure, the payments this way?
 Are we really supposed to believe that a sponsor associated with a company generating $8bn in revenue could only justify £10m a year for a Premier League club that was already winning multiple trophies at this point?
 For context, that figure is comparable to the value of Burnley’s W88 shirt sponsorship (in 2024).
 If the sponsorship was genuinely worth £80m on the open market, why was there any need for the owner to fund such a substantial proportion of it?
 The fair market value seems much closer to £80m than £10m. And if that’s the case, the funding structure raises an obvious question, what was the point?
 That’s what I find so puzzling. On the face of it, there seems to have been little commercial reason to structure the payments this way, which makes the arrangement all the more bizarre.
 One possible explanation is that City genuinely believed they had found a legitimate financial or regulatory loophole and the premier league disagree.
 I’m genuinely interested in other serious explanations.

text:
TV’s Natalie Pike: I turned detective to catch my stalker
“Long before Manchester City became a club besieged, Natalie Pike established herself as a face of its watershed moments, hosting the club’s homecoming parade from Istanbul after winning the Treble and conducting a poignant last interview with Pep Guardiola as he signed off his decade in charge. The Etihad Stadium was so comfortingly familiar that it became her sanctuary. That was until February 21 this year, when, in the midst of presenting pitchside during City’s 2-1 win over Newcastle, she grew conscious of a man hovering uncomfortably close to the barriers, intent on spooking her. “I just had a sense that something wasn’t right,” she says. “So I looked over my shoulder, and I instantly saw him – the man from the picture.”
 This picture was one she had excavated from Instagram, in a burst of panic about a traumatic episode eight days earlier. On that occasion, Pike, emerging from a restful spa day with a friend, had turned on her telephone to see a spate of missed calls from her hairdresser and the school attended by her eight-year-old son, Reggie. Two men, it turned out, had pulled up outside the salon in a van, telling staff that they knew Pike was a customer and demanding to know where she lived. The hairdresser alerted the school, conscious that it was on the same village road. “My friend said that I just went white,” she reflects. “I had no idea what it could mean. So I did what we tend to do as women, and I started investigating myself.”
 As a former model and now a versatile football presenter across BBC Sport, TNT Sports and CBS in the United States, the 43-year-old has built a substantial online presence. And when she trawled through previously hidden Instagram messages from people she did not follow, she noticed a high number across 18 months from one particular account. “They began in the usual way: ‘Happy birthday’, ‘You’re beautiful’, that kind of thing. Then they started deteriorating. So I took a screenshot of this person’s profile, sent it to my hairdresser, and she instantly confirmed it was the same man she had seen.” It would also be the same man who so unsettled her at City, although by the time she had a clear view he was bounding up the stairs to the concourse, desperate to avoid detection.
 Despite her increased prominence on television, Pike had never entertained the idea she could be the victim of stalking. She had also never intended to discuss the ordeal openly. “Whenever I’m on screen, you’ll see me very bubbly, smiley, happy,” she says. “But I’m also a very private person. My family and friends have encouraged me to do this, because I almost don’t want to admit that these things are real.” 
 Amid her maelstrom of emotions at the Etihad, she faced the same conundrum. Was there a possibility of mistaken identity? After the scare at the salon, she had contacted police, who duly tracked down the man she had discovered on social media and warned him to stay away from her. Or did she trust her instincts and decide that it was the same tormentor?
 “I ran up to the public address announcer’s room, and I had my first experience of a panic attack,” she says. “I stood in a corner, burst out crying, and I just couldn’t catch my breath. Police took it seriously, and through the stadium CCTV they were able to pinpoint him. There was a moment when they traced his steps coming into the ground, and it was harrowing to watch. He never took his eyes off me. He came in at the back of the stand and then, over a 20-minute period, moved down and stopped several times until he was about a metre away from me.”
 From there, the response was unusually swift by the standards of stalking cases. In the UK, only about six per cent of recorded offences end in a suspect being charged, while under two per cent ever result in a criminal conviction. Although Pike finds such figures “frightening”, she considers herself amongst the fortunate few. “That’s one of the reasons I wanted to speak out about this,” she explains. “The police immediately took it seriously. They arrested the guy the morning after the match, they came to my house to take my full statement, and they just went full steam ahead from there. I later found out that he had been messaging my best friend, her husband, plus other people I know. When police went through his devices, they found pictures of him sitting in the pub around the corner from my house. There were even photographs of my ex-husband’s car.”
 It is not the first stalking ordeal suffered by a high-profile female sports presenter in this country. Last year Laura Woods described to Telegraph Sport how she had been bombarded for three years by an obsessed female Liverpool fan, who would send her birthday cards that read: “Today’s the day you were born and tonight’s the night you’re going to die.” The woman was later jailed for 14 months. 
 For all that Pike has hesitated about sharing her own experience, she wants to lay bare the fear and isolation that stalkers can cause their victims. “In my head, I was minimising this as a way of trying to protect myself,” she says. “But we shouldn’t minimise these things. You have to make sure that people know this behaviour isn’t OK.”
 Although the realisation her stalker had been caught proved cathartic, his subsequent release on bail – with strict conditions not to go near her – coincided with perhaps the worst day of her life. “I asked my parents to come around so that I could fill them in on everything that was happening,” she recalls. “My mum has stage-four bowel cancer. And as I told her about the stalking, she collapsed. I scrambled an ambulance, and she ended up in hospital for five weeks. The stalking came on top of an incredibly difficult year for my family, magnifying the pressure and anxiety.”
 It came as a tonic that she soon obtained a stalking protection order against the man, which prohibited him from visiting her village, approaching any of her relatives or friends, or attending the Etihad. Manchester City took the extra precaution of banning him in any case. In the months that followed, Pike did everything she could to make herself difficult to trace, changing her car number plate, avoiding the local shops, and varying her routes home. She also derived support from the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, the UK’s leading authority on stalking and one that provides a national helpline.
 “One of the sad things about this is that it has really affected my enjoyment of going to the Etihad,” she says. “I’m a lifelong Manchester City fan, and it would always be my place of safety. I was there throughout my divorce, the pandemic, all the awful things that happen in life, and I could still be happy there. I feel like that has been taken away from me.”
 Her route into football broadcasting was, to put it mildly, unorthodox. In the early 2000s, Pike initially gained recognition at the peak of the lads’ mags era, winning FHM’s award as “High Street Honey of the Year”. It is a period that seems as though it belongs in a time capsule, especially given the recent testimony of Natalie Imbruglia, the Australian pop star, that she felt “exploited” and “traumatised” by a photoshoot for one such magazine. Pike, by contrast, insists that she felt no discomfort. “I very much look back on it with affection. Now and again, somebody will bring it up as a form of ‘gotcha’, but I’m not ashamed of it. I’m proud of it and it has brought me to where I am today.
 “Would I make those decisions now, as a 43-year-old mother? No, I wouldn’t. But I was 21. And I’m not going to allow anybody to make me feel shame for anything I’ve done in my career, then or now. That’s another reason why I want to tell my story, because it’s about showing that women are strong, that we won’t be stopped or discouraged.”
 It would be another decade before she cultivated her first opportunities in sport. “My only regret,” she says, “is that I didn’t have the self-belief to do it 20 years ago.” Having modelled the Manchester City kit for the 2008-09 campaign, the first of the Abu Dhabi-controlled era, she was eventually entrusted with being the club’s main in-house presenter, interviewing everybody from Guardiola to Liam Gallagher. She has covered every twist of the past 15 years’ transformation, now the subject of the fiercest scrutiny after the Premier League’s verdict last week that it was all achieved through artificially inflated commercial revenue. City employees are restricted from speaking about the case until the appeal is complete.
 Expanding her platform beyond City, Pike, who was born in Edinburgh, took a lead in broadcasting Scotland’s extraordinary takeover of Boston at this year’s World Cup. “I really needed this,” she said at the time, even if nobody knew the full reasons why it meant so much to her.
 Pike becomes tearful as she reflects on her Massachusetts summer, which provided a precious escape from the state of hyper-vigilance her stalker had forced her to adopt. “It makes me emotional thinking about it, because it came at the perfect time, and it was such a release from everything else that was happening,” she says. “It helps restore faith in human nature, I guess.”
 In a Manchester courtroom last Friday, she was finally able to close the book on an anguished episode, as the man who had hounded her received a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months. She had the option of asking for a screen to separate herself from the stalker, she declined, choosing instead to deliver her victim impact statement directly to him. “I did that as a means of taking back power in that situation,” she says. “I thought, ‘I don’t need to hide. I’ve got nothing to hide about’. Seeing him sentenced, and hearing the judge emphasise the seriousness of the case, I felt strong. And I felt an overwhelming relief that I could now get on with my life.”
 What happened to her has changed her profoundly, casting a shadow that has taken the best part of a year to lift. But she trusts that by telling people, she might help illuminate stalking’s true toll and the human scars that can lie beneath even the most ebullient personas on screen.”

text:
Manchester City chair shielded by diplomatic immunity [via @FT] (paywalled article)
Unfortunately the above article is paywalled. I have made best efforts to bypass but cannot on this occasion. If anyone has the full article please share in a comment below, and I can update the description here. 
 I have managed to source the article and post below, thank you. Please consider supporting journalism where necessary.
 Synopsis from @City_Xtra
 Khaldoon Al Mubarak was placed on the UK’s official list of approved diplomats in 2020, automatically granting the #ManCity chairman immunity from any criminal investigation and in most cases shields the person from civil proceedings on UK soil.
 [via @FT]
 ————————————
 Manchester City’s Emirati chair was granted diplomatic immunity six years ago in a move that could complicate any legal action resulting from findings that the Premier League club artificially inflated its finances by more than £900mn.
 Khaldoon al-Mubarak, a senior Abu Dhabi official who has chaired City since 2008, was placed on the UK’s official list of approved diplomats in 2020. This automatically confers immunity from any criminal investigation and in most cases shields the person from civil proceedings on UK soil.
 The Premier League said on Tuesday that an independent commission had found City guilty of all charges relating to serious breaches of its financial rules, following an investigation that was launched in 2018.
 The club, owned by a member of Abu Dhabi’s royal family since 2008, “concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators” to circumvent spending limits between 2009 and 2018, the league said. City strongly denies the charges and will appeal against the decision. 
 The findings, if upheld, could open the door to further legal proceedings, which has been a source of concern for City, according to two people familiar with the situation. This could include civil action from other Premier League clubs that believe they have lost out on the pitch as a result of City’s actions.
 There is also the potential for criminal investigations by the Serious Fraud Office, the police or other agencies, according to lawyers not involved in the case.
 There is no suggestion of personal wrongdoing by Mubarak, who is one of the United Arab Emirates’ president’s most trusted advisers and is also the chief executive of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign fund, Mubadala.
 One senior UK government figure said it would be “very odd” if somebody in Mubarak’s position did not have diplomatic status, given that he has chaired Abu Dhabi’s Executive Affairs Authority, the equivalent of the UK’s Cabinet Office, since 2006. “He’s diplomatically in charge of the UK file as well as the China file . . . and he’s the main liaison with the US administration,” the person said.
 Mubarak’s diplomatic immunity could complicate follow-up legal action against the club, according to lawyers, as it largely protects an individual from being sued or charged in a criminal probe in the country where he or she is an emissary. If the SFO were to pursue a criminal case, it would be required to do so under fraud laws that applied at the time of the alleged wrongdoing and that require prosecutors to prove the “directing mind” of the corporate entity was complicit.
 Nick Vamos, former head of extradition at the Crown Prosecution Service, said that as well as having full protection from criminal prosecution, Mubarak “would also have immunity from civil actions relating to his ‘official functions’.” He added that “there could be some debate about whether the activities in question were part of those functions or purely private matters”.
 The independent commission found City used a private company controlled by owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, who also holds senior roles in the UAE’s government, to dramatically augment fees paid by legitimate commercial sponsors.
 The club’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, said on Tuesday that the “whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation: that the owners’ personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true. Irrefutable evidence has been provided to the Premier League commission that shows this could not happen and that it did not happen.”
 Mubarak, who regularly attends City matches, said in a statement at the weekend: “While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity.”
 Individuals on the diplomatic list are largely immune from civil litigation. In a key test case in the English courts in 2016, the former prime minister of Qatar Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim Bin Jaber Al Thani, known as HBJ, successfully argued in a separate case that he could not be sued in England because of his diplomatic immunity.
 Independent legal experts said that criminal proceedings against City were possible where the Premier League has found failings related to financial dealings. Tom Forster KC, a financial crime barrister, said that “if there is evidence of systemic false accounting and other Companies Act offences then there is a significant risk that both the corporate vehicle and individuals may face a criminal investigation and prosecution”.
 Publicly available lists show Mubarak appearing as an official of the UAE’s embassy in London in 2022. However, UK officials told the FT that the UAE had notified the government of Mubarak’s diplomatic status in 2020. The commission’s findings threaten to strain relations between the UK and the UAE.
 In 2021, the two countries launched a sovereign investment partnership, with Mubadala the lead investor. The agreement has since generated £30bn in investment commitments from the UAE into Britain, overseen by Mubarak. The UAE foreign ministry and Manchester City did not respond to requests for comment.
 Credit: Josh Noble (FT article writer)

text:
Andy Burnham, UK Prime Minister: "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up & "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city" [BBC News]
Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.
 The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.
 An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.
 The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.
 It comes as the Independent Football Regulator – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".
 The regulator suggested it would be exploring options – including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club – once the disciplinary process was completed.
 Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.
 The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".
 The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.
 The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.
 Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years.
 Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them.
 "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."
 Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester until June, added: "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city".
 He said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners when he was mayor would stand up to scrutiny.
 Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.
 Burnham was speaking to the BBC from Hill Dickinson Stadium, the home of Everton, the team he supports.
 Everton had their own run in with Premier League financial rules when they were charged and deducted 10 points for more minor breaches in November 2023, reduced to six on appeal.
 Burnham said: "Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation because I still hold the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process."
 Drawing a comparison between that and City's current predicament, he added: "I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and with hindsight I think more people would say that wasn't fair, the way that was handled.
 "So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."
 It is "frustrating when people rush to judgement", Burnham said.
 He accepted there was "a lot at stake" for City fans, the club and Manchester itself.
 But he added it would be wrong for him to intervene.
 City have said in a statement they are "both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission" and maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.

text:
There are strong suggestions that club representatives were invited to sign non-disclosure agreements this week before allegedly being told by the league's leading figures - one can only presume Richard Masters(CEO) and Alison Brittain, the chair - what verdict the independent commission had reached
When finally the verdict of Manchester City’s guilt leaked on Friday, the idea bloomed of a Premier League dissolving into competing claims that might usher in a wholesale reordering of history, and of compensation. Compensation to be payable for trophies not won, league positions not achieved, European campaigns not embarked upon and many other grievances besides.
 As for the reality, that may well be different. Only four clubs in September 2024 were even prepared to instruct their own legal counsel to notify City Football Group (CFG) that they reserved the right to seek compensation in the event of the Premier League charges being upheld. It does not say much about the commitment of the rest, and you would be hard-pressed to say that even among the four that did, the conviction to go through with it has grown in the interim.
 They left it late – waiting until the six-year limit from the first disclosure of the allegations against City in the German media in 2018 had almost expired. It was not simple from the start. The Premier League would not even tell the four – Tottenham Hotspur, Arsenal, Manchester United and Liverpool – the identity of the three individuals on the independent commission so they might be contacted directly. All communication had to go through the league – and the commission was not prepared to add the question of compensation to its own scope of judgment. The clubs were obliged to contact CFG individually.
 From the traditional big six, Chelsea declined to take part. So too did 14 others in the Premier League that season, all of whom – should they decide to take retrospective legal action against City in the event of a guilty verdict on most of those charges – will now find the legal bar that much higher.
 The power of Abu Dhabi and its investments is strong. How many of those club owners who might otherwise have signed up with those four seeking compensation instead considered the importance to their own financial picture of Mubadala, the sovereign wealth fund chaired by Khaldoon Al-Mubarak, the CFG chairman, and then thought better of it?
 The people who own the Premier League clubs outside the elite have investors to appease and partners to keep onside. There is independence of a sort, of course, and necessary legal separations. But money has a way of finding its way across borders and jurisdictions, of exerting its power formally and informally across all sectors and all interests.
 Of course, CFG will always say that the investment in City is by a private individual – Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed – via the investment vehicle Abu Dhabi United Group. But as the brother of the president of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed, one can take a view on that.
 Of those four clubs that did reserve the right to seek compensation in 2024, two are now under radically different leadership. Spurs and Arsenal were previously led by experienced boardroom heavyweights, both of whom – Daniel Levy and Tim Lewis – departed one year ago. Levy, the longest-serving chairman in the league, and Lewis, a former corporate lawyer who had been a fierce advocate of financial controls, were capable of a stubbornness that would have been difficult for CFG. Both were effectively dethroned last year by a younger generation of the families that owned their respective clubs.
 As for Liverpool, Billy Hogan, the chief executive, is a Fenway Sports Group stalwart and the smart money is that FSG will not still be in control at Anfield by the time that this case is resolved definitively. What the new consortium waiting in the wings makes of it all, led by Amit Bhatia, the British-Indian investor, with Jeff Bezos, the Amazon billionaire, among his backers, only time will tell.
 Below the millionaire and billionaire owner class there is a cadre of executives, some of whom have done their time at CFG. Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, is not the only man to have burnished his reputation at CFG. Jason Wilcox is another CFG man at United. While United have reserved the right to pursue City for compensation, it must have been an awkward personal call for Berrada. Spurs too have hired several CFG people, including Ryan Norys, the chief revenue officer, who left this week.
 As for any idea that CFG would, over the weekend, simply bow to the general sense of anger that the guilty verdict unleashed on Friday, that was comprehensively dismissed by the tone of the statement from CFG chairman Khaldoon.
 It did not sound like a man who was about to stand down his legal team after three-and-a-half years of finding every way possible to dismantle the institution of financial controls that his and 19 other clubs had voted for in years previous. “The Premier League process still has a long way to run,” Khaldoon declared – and he should know. Not a step backwards in terms of the club’s longstanding claim of total innocence. This is the point where we say that City denies all the charges.
 To say there is a general anxiety about the Premier League’s position on the process of disclosing the verdict and that of its 19 other clubs would be an understatement. There are strong suggestions that club representatives were invited to sign non-disclosure agreements this week before allegedly being told by the league’s leading figures – one can only presume Richard Masters, the chief executive, and Alison Brittain, the chair – what verdict the independent commission had reached. As for checking the substance of that, unfortunately no one at the Premier League is prepared to discuss any of it.
 One might have expected clubs to be readying themselves for a reckoning with CFG once all this is over. Everton faced a major compensation claim from Burnley over their own profit and sustainability rules breach in 2024, which came in the season in which Burnley were relegated. That only four agreed to do so says much. Chelsea will have known then that they had their own problems – and the leniency the club was shown by the Premier League and Football Association suggests that the fatigue of the City case was a useful leverage.
 Friday’s leaked verdict electrified a case stuck behind closed doors for so long, but it did not signal the end of City’s determination to attack the rules it signed up to compete under. As for the rest, one should not expect them to throw themselves into a compensation battle against an opponent that fights on all fronts.
 [Sam Wallace, Telegraph]

text:
Manchester City found guilty: What comes next?
The next step will be a sanctioning process and the commission will be able to impose a range of penalties. City are able to appeal the verdict, as Everton and Nottingham Forest both did when found to have breached PSR in the last three years.
 “Unless it can successfully argue otherwise, the appeal would operate as a review of the first instance proceedings, not a full rehearing,” says Alex Goodchild, Associate at specialist entertainment and sports law firm Bray & Krais.
 “And given the exceptional scale of the case, with the original hearing spanning 12 weeks and covering nine seasons of evidence, it is hard to see the Appeal Board granting leave to adduce fresh evidence.
 “If the appeal fails, the only remaining avenue would be an arbitration challenge on very limited grounds — such as the decision being ultra vires, tainted by bad faith, arising from serious procedural error, or irrational – each of which carries a very high bar. Subject to narrow exceptions, that tribunal’s decision would be final.”
 There is also the very real prospect of City’s rivals taking their own action if the appeal process does not see verdicts overturned. Clubs including Liverpool and Manchester United missed out on Premier League titles during the years of City’s alleged breaches and the financial rewards that come with it. Others might consider City’s actions had blocked them from lucrative European qualification and seek their own compensation.
 Burnley’s recent case against Everton will certainly embolden those clubs. A commission awarded Burnley £26m in damages, plus a further £9m in interest, after it was argued that Everton’s PSR breach in the 2021-22 season impacted Burnley’s attempts to avoid Premier League relegation. Everton will appeal that financial penalty but there is now a clear precedent for aggrieved clubs to pursue compensation.

Explaining the charges against Man City
Manchester City — Charges Breakdown
  Accurate Financial Information — 54 charges
  📅 2009–10 to 2017–18
 Alleged failure to provide accurate financial information giving a true and fair view of the club's financial position, including revenue, sponsorship revenue, related parties and operating costs.
  Manager & Player Remuneration — 14 charges
  📅 Manager: 2009–10 to 2012–13
 📅 Players: 2010–11 to 2015–16
 Alleged failure to provide full details of remuneration in relevant manager and player contracts.
  UEFA Regulations / FFP — 5 charges
  📅 2013–14 to 2017–18
 Alleged failure to comply with Premier League rules requiring clubs to comply with UEFA regulations, including Financial Fair Play rules.
  Premier League PSR — 7 charges
  📅 2015–16 to 2017–18
 Alleged breaches of the Premier League's Profitability and Sustainability Rules.
  Failure to Cooperate — 35 charges
  📅 December 2018 to February 2023
 Alleged failure to cooperate with and assist the Premier League's investigation, including providing documents and information.
 Total: charges
 Note: These are allegations made by the Premier League and should not be treated as established findings.
 Detailed Breakdown by Category
  Failure to Provide Accurate Financial Information — 54 Charges
  Timeframe: 2009–10 to 2017–18
 The Premier League alleges that Manchester City failed to provide accurate financial information giving a “true and fair view” of the club's financial position.
 The information covered areas including:
 Revenue
 Sponsorship revenue
 Related-party transactions
 Operating costs
 The Premier League's formal charge does not itself establish that owner investment was disguised as sponsorship income. However, reporting surrounding the case has connected these allegations to claims arising from leaked documents concerning sponsorship arrangements involving companies including Etihad and Etisalat and alleged funding from the club's ownership group. These should therefore be described as reported allegations, rather than established facts.
  Manager & Player Remuneration — 14 Charges
  Manager Remuneration — 8 Charges
 Timeframe: 2009–10 to 2012–13
 The Premier League alleges that City failed to include full details of manager remuneration in the relevant contracts during these four seasons.
 Reports surrounding the case have linked this part of the allegations to former manager Roberto Mancini and a reported consultancy arrangement involving Abu Dhabi-based club Al Jazira.
 Player Remuneration — 6 Charges
 Timeframe: 2010–11 to 2015–16
 The Premier League alleges that City failed to include full details of player remuneration in relevant player contracts during these six seasons.
 There have been reports about particular players and alleged additional payments, including claims concerning image rights and other arrangements. However, the formal Premier League charge does not publicly establish that all six charges specifically involved offshore image-rights agreements.
  UEFA Regulations / Financial Fair Play — 5 Charges
  Timeframe: 2013–14 to 2017–18
 The Premier League alleges that City breached rules requiring clubs to comply with UEFA regulations, including UEFA's Club Licensing and Financial Fair Play regulations, during five seasons.
 These allegations are connected to the broader financial-information allegations, but the charge itself concerns compliance with the Premier League rules requiring adherence to UEFA regulations
 .
  Premier League Profitability & Sustainability Rules — 7 Charges
  Timeframe: 2015–16 to 2017–18
 The Premier League alleges that City breached its Profitability and Sustainability Rules (PSR) during these three seasons.
 The important distinction is that the formal charge alleges breaches of the applicable PSR rules. It is safer not to state as an established fact that City's “true accounts” would have produced losses above the permitted threshold, because that is part of the substance of the allegations being contested.
  Failure to Cooperate With the Investigation — 35 Charges
  Timeframe: December 2018 to February 2023
 The Premier League alleges that City failed to cooperate with and assist its investigation, including failing to provide requested documents and information in accordance with the applicable rules.

Manchester City keep entertaining. Maresca is learning to love the chaos
Enzo Maresca summed up his feelings about Manchester City’s chaotic 5-3 victory over Sunderland in a way that many might expect. “To be honest, I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3,” he smiled.
 Maresca arrived with a reputation for slow, methodical football. He threatened to walk out on Leicester City after fans groaned at his possession-based approach, despite his side being top of the Championship by 10 points in January 2024 — and many took Chelsea player Cole Palmer’s recent reference to ‘safe zones’ as an attack on the Italian’s preference for structure.
 Even sources close to City’s first team in recent years, familiar with Maresca’s style of play as an opposition manager, believed he was more suited to the City side that won the treble in 2022-23, rather than the more dynamic squad of players that they have assembled since.
 And while there is plenty for City to improve upon, having been given the runaround by Brian Brobbey and almost conceding a comedy own goal that would have made it 4-4 on Sunday, Maresca’s City side are looking like entertainers at this early stage — and that could be the theme of their season.
